# Overview

A surprising amount of the data on Kaggle isn't real. Some of it is openly
synthetic (generated to look like a real dataset), some is simulated from a
textbook or a model, some is a real dataset that has been quietly padded,
duplicated, or "cleaned" beyond recognition, and some is exactly what it claims
to be. It's easy to get several hours into an analysis before you realize the
patterns you're describing were never in the world at all.

In this project you'll build that instinct on purpose. You'll pick one dataset,
investigate how it was really produced, and make a **data-driven argument** about
whether it reflects a genuine data-collection process or was fabricated,
simulated, or synthetically generated.

**The verdict is not the point of the project. The evidence is.** A careful
report that concludes "I found strong but not conclusive signs this is synthetic"
&mdash; or "this is real, but it has serious data-quality problems that would
have bitten me later" &mdash; earns full marks if the investigation is good. What
you're being graded on is whether you can use `ggplot2` and basic wrangling to
interrogate a dataset and reason about it under uncertainty.

## What your report should contain

Keep it short &mdash; about 3 pages if rendered to PDF.

1. **Introduction** &mdash; one paragraph: what the dataset is, where on Kaggle
   you found it (link), what it claims to be, and what its data card / description
   says about where it came from.
2. **At least three lines of evidence.** Each one is a short subsection with:
   - the question you're asking of the data ("do the ages cluster on round
     numbers?", "should these two columns agree, and do they?"),
   - a single graph *or* summary table that addresses it,
   - two or three sentences on what it shows and how it moves your thinking.
3. **Verdict** &mdash; your best judgment, stated with a confidence level (e.g.
   "likely synthetic", "probably real but poorly documented", "genuinely can't
   tell, and here's why"), justified by the evidence above.
4. **Reflection** &mdash; one short paragraph: if you'd found this out on day one,
   how would it change what you'd do with this dataset next? Or: what would you
   need from the dataset's authors to be confident?

Your rendered file should **not** `echo` the code, but the code in your `.qmd`
should be clean and readable.

## Lines of inquiry to try

You don't need all of these, and a good project usually goes deep on a few rather
than shallow on all. We'll work through several of these together in class.

- **Distributions that are too clean** &mdash; suspiciously uniform, perfectly
  bell-shaped, no outliers, variance that doesn't grow with the mean the way it
  usually does in real measurements.
- **Impossible or contradictory records** &mdash; a `0` where a `0` can't happen
  (zero blood pressure, zero price), an end date before a start date, a total
  that doesn't equal the sum of its parts, a city in the wrong state.
- **Duplicates and near-duplicates** &mdash; exact repeated rows, or rows that
  differ only in an ID. Real collection produces some; a lot is a red flag.
- **Round-number clustering** &mdash; humans and generators both love round
  numbers, but real instruments usually don't.
- **Decimal precision** &mdash; every value to exactly two decimals, or a column
  of "measurements" with more precision than any real instrument would give.
- **Correlation structure** &mdash; variables that *should* be related in the
  real world (height and weight, price and size) but aren't, or vice versa.
- **Categorical balance** &mdash; categories split almost exactly evenly, or a
  grouping variable with implausibly equal group sizes.
- **Time structure** &mdash; timestamps at perfectly regular intervals, no
  weekday/weekend effect, no gaps.
- **External benchmarks** &mdash; does the mean / range / proportion match what
  you can look up about the real world?
- **The paper trail** &mdash; the data card, the uploader's other datasets, a
  cited source you can go check, a "generated with" note in the description.

# Dataset shortlist

Pick one of these, **or** bring your own (see below). Download the CSV from
Kaggle and commit it to the `data/` folder of your project repo.

Your report should not just repeat what someone else concluded &mdash; if you
find a discussion of the dataset's authenticity online, cite it, but the analysis
must be your own.

1. **Medical Cost Personal Datasets** (`insurance.csv`) &mdash;
   <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance>. Age, sex, BMI,
   number of children, smoker status, region, and annual medical charges for
   ~1,300 people.
2. **Students Performance in Exams** &mdash;
   <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/spscientist/students-performance-in-exams>.
   Demographic fields plus math, reading, and writing scores for 1,000 students.
3. **Pima Indians Diabetes Database** &mdash;
   <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/pima-indians-diabetes-database>. Eight
   clinical measurements and a diabetes outcome for 768 women.
4. **Red Wine Quality (Cortez et al., 2009)** &mdash;
   <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/red-wine-quality-cortez-et-al-2009>.
   Eleven physicochemical measurements and a quality rating for ~1,600 Portuguese
   wines.
5. **Superstore Sales** &mdash; search Kaggle for "Superstore dataset" (e.g.
   `vivek468/superstore-dataset-final`). ~10,000 retail orders with customer,
   product, geography, sales, and profit fields.
6. **Spotify Tracks Dataset** &mdash;
   <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/maharshipandya/-spotify-tracks-dataset>.
   Audio features (danceability, tempo, loudness, &hellip;), popularity, and
   genre for a large sample of tracks.

*Also worth a look:* the "Heart Disease Dataset" reuploads on Kaggle, which vary
a lot in size &mdash; comparing two of them can itself be a line of evidence.

## Bring your own

If none of these grab you, choose your own Kaggle dataset, subject to:

- at least **6 variables**, with at least **2 quantitative** and **2
  categorical**,
- at least **500 rows**,
- provenance that is **genuinely ambiguous** &mdash; do not pick a dataset whose
  description already tells you it's synthetic, and don't pick something so
  famous the answer is common knowledge,
- **run your choice by me on Ed before you start** so I know the dataset.

# Submission

Work in a `quarto` file. Render to `gfm`, `pdf`, or `html`. I'll distribute a
GitHub skeleton repo; fill it in as you work, commit your final `.qmd` and
rendered output, and link the repo to Gradescope. Give your report an informative
title.

# Rubric

A **successful** project will:

- [ ] Include all necessary components pushed to GitHub and linked to Gradescope
    - There should be at least two commits with substantial changes between them
- [ ] Contain code, graphs, and written summary in a single `.qmd` document
- [ ] The `.qmd` contains all necessary code for recreation and no unnecessary code
- [ ] The rendered document does **not** echo the code
- [ ] Use a dataset that meets the requirements above, with genuinely ambiguous
      provenance (not self-declared synthetic)
- [ ] State what the dataset claims to be and where it was found
- [ ] Present **at least three distinct lines of evidence**, each supported by a
      graph or a summary table
- [ ] Interpret the evidence correctly &mdash; written claims match what the
      graph or table actually shows
- [ ] Use at least two different `geom`s across the report
- [ ] Reach a clear verdict with a stated confidence level, justified by the
      evidence (a well-argued "I can't be sure" is acceptable)
- [ ] Meet minimum submission quality standards
    - Very few grammatical mistakes, spelling mistakes, or typos
    - Informative report title; readable theme; appropriate labels and font sizes
    - No package-loading messages, warnings, or other clutter in the output

An **excellent** project will meet all of the requirements for a successful
project, plus

- [ ] At least one line of evidence goes beyond single-variable distributions
      &mdash; e.g. a cross-variable consistency check, correlation structure that
      should or shouldn't exist, duplicate / near-duplicate detection, decimal or
      digit-pattern analysis, or a comparison to an external real-world benchmark
- [ ] At least one graph uses two or more layers, or a `ggplot2` element beyond
      what we covered in class
- [ ] Graphs use a consistent theme customized beyond a full theme (e.g. past
      `theme_minimal()`), and at least one graph uses a custom `scale_` element
- [ ] The reflection genuinely engages with the "so what" &mdash; how an early
      finding would have changed the downstream analysis, or what would be needed
      to resolve the ambiguity
- [ ] A clear commit history that shows the investigation developing
- [ ] Meet high submission quality standards (no typos; polished throughout)

::: callout-note
## On not being sure

For some datasets you will not be able to *prove* anything &mdash; that's
realistic, and it's fine. Grade yourself on whether your evidence is varied and
correctly read and your argument is honest about its own limits. And remember
only 2 of the 3 portfolio projects need to hit "excellent" for an A, so it's OK
to decide a given dataset isn't giving you enough to work with and say so.
:::

# Can I work with someone?

This is an **individual** portfolio project. You may brainstorm, get feedback on
graphs, and get conceptual debugging help, but the analysis and writing must be
your own. Cite any resources you use (title, author, link, and one line on what
you used it for).

A note/reminder on AI: *Large-language models (e.g. ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) should
only be used for coding or debugging help after you've attempted to solve the
problem on your own. You should never copy and paste any course materials into a
large-language model, and you should never copy and paste anything out of a
large-language model into your course materials. Copying, paraphrasing,
summarizing, or submitting work generated by anyone but yourself without proper
attribution is considered academic dishonesty (this includes output from LLMs).
You are not allowed to upload datasets or assignment prompts into a large
language model.*
